la:adj:immundus.html:
immundus (inm-), a, um, adj.
inmundus
,
unclean, impure, dirty, filthy, foul (syn.: spurcus, obscenus, impurus).
Lit. (class.): humus erat immunda, lutulenta vino, ap. : homo,; , 115; ; : canis,: Harpyiae contactu immundo omnia foedant,: sues,: popinae,: ager,run wild, overgrown,: pauperies domūs,.—Absol.: im-mundae, ārum, f., unclean women, .—Comp.: superne deciduo immundiore lapsu aliquo polluta,: nilo mundius hoc, niloque immundior ille,; .—Sup.: liquet illos immundissimos fuisse,; .—*
Trop.: aut immunda crepent ignominiosaque dicta,.—Adv.: immundē, impurely, uncleanly: foedare templa, Jul. .

la:adv:immo.gloss: on the contrary, nay (rather), no indeed
senses: on the contrary, nay (rather), no indeed
actually, what is more, even (often intensified with edepol, hercle, ecastor, vero, potius, etc.)
la:adv:immo.html:
immo, incorrectly written īmo
perh. sup. form from in, with ending mo; cf.: summus, primus; hence
,
on the contrary, no indeed, by no means, or yes indeed, by all means (more commonly contradicting or essentially qualifying what precedes; but never, like minime, as an independent negative, being regularly accompanied by a clause defining the meaning; v. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 551).
Lit.
In gen.: Tr. Etiam fatetur de hospite? Th. Immo pernegat, : An. Ubi? domin'? Ch. Immo apud libertum Discum, : Do. Hae quid ad me? To. Immo ad te attinent, : De. Faciat, ut voles. Nau. Immo ejus judicio permitto omnia, ; .—Esp., in a reply extending or amplifying the preceding thought (cf.: potius, quin potius): expedies? nempe ut modo? D. Immo melius spero, ; : Si. Quid? hoc intellextin'? an nondum etiam ne hoc quidem? Da. Immo callide, : non igitur faciat, dixerit quis, quod utile sit, quod expediat? Immo intelligat nihil nec expedire nec utile esse, quod sit injustum,: causa igitur non bona est? Immo optima,; cf.: quem hominem? levem? immo gravissimum. Mobilem? immo constantissimum. Familiarem? immo alienissimum,; : cum ille dixisset, se vero non exspectare; Immo, inquit, rogo exspectes,: quid tu? Nullane habes vitia? Immo alia. Et fortasse minora?; .—So in retorting a question: Me.

Quid apud hasce aedes negotii est tibi? So. Immo quid tibi'st? ; : Ph. An amabo meretrix illa est, quae illam sustulit? La. Immo meretrix fuit; sed ut sit, de ea re eloquar,; cf. : Si. Paucis te volo. So. Dictum puta: Nempe ut curentur recte haec. Si. Immo aliud, .—

Strengthened by edepol, hercle, ecastor, vero, potius, etc.: Ol. Ecquid amas nunc me? St. Immo edepol me quam te minus, ; : St. Quod bonum atque fortunatum mihi sit. Ol. Ita vero et mihi. Ch. Non. Ol. Immo hercle. Ch. Immo mihi hercle, ; : Pa. Mala es. Ph. Immo ecastor, : Pa. Nescis, Parmeno, Quantum hodie profueris mihi, etc. ... Par. Immo vero scio, neque hoc imprudens feci, : quid? si tyrannidem occupare, si patriam prodere conabitur pater: silebitne filius? Immo vero obsecrabit patrem, ne id faciat,; : Tr. Sub dio coli absque sole perpetuum diem. Si. Immo edepol vero, cum, etc., : Tr. Ecquid placent? Th. Ecquid placeant me rogas? immo hercle vero perplacent, : senatus haec intelligit, consul videt: hic tamen vivit. Vivit? immo vero etiam in senatum venit,; : De. Juben' hanc hinc abscedere? Ph. Immo intus potius, : immo hercle abiero potius,: sed vos nihilne attulistis inde auri domum? Immo etiam,: immo etiam,; : immo vero etiam, v. above: immo est quoque,: an infirmissimi omnium tamquam, quos nuper subjecit, Dolopes? Immo contra ea, etc.,: immo contra,; ; .—
In partic.
As an expression of dislike or surprise (ante-class.): Ch. Verum vis dicam? Da. Immo etiam Narrationis incipit mihi initium, no indeed! now he is going to begin a long story, : idne est verum? immo id est genus hominum pessimum,: Pe. Euge, euge, lepide: laudo commentum tuum. Pa. Ut, si illanc concriminatus sit advorsum Militem, etc. ... Pe. Immo optume, no! capital! .—
Immo si scias or immo si audias, if you only knew, had only heard, intimating that such is not the case (ante-class.): immo si scias,: St. Scelestissimum Me esse credo. Pa. Immo si scias dicta, quae dixit hodie, ; : Ly. Bene hercle factum et gaudeo. De. Immo si scias, ; so ellipt.,; : immo si audias Meas pugnas, fugias demissis manibus domum,.—
Transf. (perh. not before the Aug. period), for vel potius, in the middle of a sentence, to correct or add emphasis to what has been said, nay rather; nay, I should rather say: immo ita sit,nay,: simulacra deum, deos immo ipsos convulsos ex sedibus suis ablatos esse,: ipse aliquid, immo multa quotidie dicat,; ; : qui pauculis diebus gestum consulatum, immo non gestum abiciebant per edictum,: nihil causae est, cur non illam vocis modulationem fidibus ac tibiis, immo hercle, cymbalis adjuvemus,; : immo vero,.—In forming a climax: quanta verborum nobis paupertas, immo egestas sit,: Agrippinam nihilo tractabiliorem, immo in dies amentiorem,; .!*? Rarely after a word in the clause (first in Livy): nihil immo,: non immo,; cf.: non habet immo suum,: vivit immo vigetque,: statueretur immo,: frueretur immo his,: quaedam immo virtutes,: illos quin immo,; cf.: ipsam quin immo curam,: quin immo,; ; ; .

la:noun:immortalitas.html:
immortālĭtas (inm-), ātis, f.
immortalis
,
exemption from death, immortality (class.).
Lit.: salvos sum: inmortalitas mihi datast,: quae Socrates supremo vitae die de immortalitate animorum disseruisset, Cic. de Sen. 21, 78: vita beata nullā aliā re nisi immortalitate cedens caelestibus,.—In plur.: vide igitur, ne virtutibus hominum isti honores habeantur, non immortalitatibus,to their immortal natures,.—
Transf.
Imperishableness, imperishable fame, undying renown, immortality: non censet lugendam esse mortem, quam immortalitas consequatur,: jam tum inmortalitatis virtute partae fautor,: emit morte immortalitatem,: mihi populus Romanus aeternitatem immortalitatemque donavit,: gloriae,: aliquid immortalitati commendare,: aliquid immortalitati tradere,. —*
(Acc. to immortalis, II. B.) Blessedness, the height of happiness: mihi immortalitas parta est, si, etc.,.

la:adj:immoderatus.html:
immŏdĕrātus (inm-), a, um, adj.
in-moderatus
,
without measure, measureless, immeasurable.
Lit. (only poet.): vides sublime, fusum, immoderatum aethera, unbounded (= immensum), Cic. poët. N. D. 2, 25, 65; .—
Trop., unrestrained, unbridled, excessive, immoderate (freq. and class.): ipsum illum Aristotelis discipulum, superbum, crudelem, immoderatum fuisse,: homo et turbulentus,: mulier,: immensae cupiditates, infinitae et immoderatae sunt,: intemperantia,: quippe duos pro uno dominos acceptos, inmoderata, infinita potestate,: res immoderata cupido est,: motus animi, cum immoderatiores sunt, vitia fiunt,: immoderatissimae luxuriae esse,: immoderato potu et pastu pars animi obstupefacta,: ne immoderata aut angusta sit oratio,: vox immoderatior, Cael. ap. : tam immoderatae linguae fuit, unbridled, Luc.: tempestates,.—Hence, adv.: immŏdĕrātē.
Lit.: without measure or rule: moveri immoderate et fortuitu,: vox immoderate profusa,: effunditur spiritus,.—
Trop., immoderately, extravagantly: vivere,: jactari,: abuti nostra facilitate,.—Comp.: ferre casum incommodorum tuorum,.—Sup.: laetari,.

la:adj:immortalis.gloss: immortal, undying, not subject to death.
senses: immortal, undying, not subject to death.
la:adj:immortalis.html:
immortālis (inm-), e, adj.
in-mortalis
,
undying, immortal (class.).
Lit.: si nullum corpus immortale sit, nullum esse corpus sempiternum: corpus autem immortale nullum esse, etc.,: credo deos immortales sparsisse animos in corpora humana, etc.,: dii; v. deus: animi,; : natura (opp. mortalis fortuna),: pro di inmortales!: pro deorum inmortalium!—Subst. plur.: immortāles, ium, m., the immortals, gods: quod ad immortales attinet, haec; deinceps quod ad mortales,to the gods, Müll.; .—
Transf.
Imperishable, eternal, endless: memoria et gloria,: memoriam alicujus reddere,: fructum cepi vestri in me amoris et judicii,: gratias agere alicui, Planc. ap. : opera edere,: tributa,: illa Sallustii velocitas,: nemo ignaviā immortalis factus est,: immortalia ne speres, monet annus, etc.,.—
Poet., like the gods, blessed, exceedingly happy: immortalis ero, si altera talis erit,; 2, 15 (3, 7), 39.—Hence, * adv.: immortā-lĭter, infinitely: gaudeo,.

la:verb:immineo.gloss: to project, bend or lean toward or over, overhang
senses: to project, bend or lean toward or over, overhang
to be eager for or intent upon, long for
to be near at hand, impend; to be imminent
la:verb:immineo.html:
immĭnĕo (inm-), ēre, v. n.
in-mineo
,
to project over or towards a thing, to bend or lean towards, to hang down over, overhang (syn. impendeo).
Lit. (mostly poet.): collis plurimus urbi Imminet,commands,; cf.: imminens prope ipsis moenibus tumulus,: imminens villae tua pinus esto,: candida populus antro Imminet,: aër his,: caelumque quod imminet orbi,: scopulus aequoribus,: apex collis subjectis arvis,: nemus desuper,: arbos,: imminet e celsis audentius improba muris Virgo,; : choros ducit Venus imminente luna,shining overhead,: cum ageretur togata, simulans, caterva tota clarissima concentione in ore impuri hominis imminens contionata est: Huic vitae tuae, etc., bending or turning towards, ; cf.: gestu omni imminenti,bent towards him,.—
Transf., to be near to a thing, to touch on, border upon.
In gen. (rare): imminet hic, sequiturque parem, similisque tenenti Non tenet,: tergo fugacis,, 542: carcer imminens foro,adjoining,: imminentia muro aedificia,.—
In partic. (like impendere and instare), in an inimical sense, to threaten, menace, by nearness or commanding position (class.): nimis imminebat propter propinquitatem Aegina Piraeeo,; cf.: Carthago imminere jam fructuosissimis insulis populi Romani videbatur,: certior sum factus, Parthos ... Ciliciae magis imminere,: imminent duo reges toti Asiae,: circum insulas Italiae inminentes,: Mithridates Italiae quoque,: Parthi Latio,: Germaniae et Britanniae,: bello subegit gentem rebus populi Romani imminentem,: instabat agmen Caesaris atque universum imminebat,: imbrium divina avis imminentŭm,: turris ingens inminebat,; : inminentes tumuli,. —
Trop. (class.).
To strive eagerly ofter a thing, to be eager for, to long for, be intent upon: hujus mendicitas aviditate conjuncta in nostras fortunas imminebat,; : in alterius ducis exercitusque opprimendi occasionem imminebat,: huc imminet: om nes Dirigit huc sensus,: alieno imminere,: rebus,: quod imminere emptioni publicanos videbat,: peritus rerum popularium imminensque ei potestati,: spei majoris honoris,: occasioni alloquendi regem,: exitio conjugis,: Verres avaritia semper hiante atque imminenti fuit,.—
Transf. (acc. to I. B.), to be near at hand, to impend.
In gen.: sunt qui ea, quae quotidie imminent, non videant,: mors, quae propter incertos casus quotidie imminet,.—
In partic., to threaten by nearness, to be imminent: periculum, quod imminere ipsi portenderetur,: periculum ambobus,: imminentes undique insidiae,: discrimina undique,: summum discrimen,: bellum,: taedio praesentium et imminentium metu,.

la:verb:imminuo.html:
immĭnŭo (inm-), ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.
inminuo
,
to lessen, diminish a thing (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. signif.; cf. diminuo, comminuo).
Lit.
In gen.: si istas exiguas copias quam minime imminueris,: pondus,.—
Pregn., to weaken, impair, enfeeble: corpus otio, animum libidinibus imminuebant,; cf.: Gauda, morbis confectus, et ob eam caussam mente paululum inminuta,: vires (Venus),; cf. .—In mal. part.: virginem,; —
Trop.
In gen., to lessen, diminish, abate: aestivorum tempus comitiorum mora imminuerat,: quod populi semper proprium fuit, quod nemo imminuit, nemo mutavit,: imminuitur aliquid de voluptate,: nihil ex consuetudine luxus atque desidiae,: postquam se dolor imminuit,: verbum imminutum,contracted,.—
In partic., pregn., to encroach upon, to violate, injure, subvert, ruin, destroy: nullum jus tam sanctum atque integrum, quod non ejus scelus atque perfidia violarit et imminuerit,: cupiditas imminuta ac debilitata,: bellum attenuatum atque imminutum,: pudicitiam,: auctoritatem,; cf. : jus legationis,, § 84: laudem alicujus,, A, 2: libertatem,: Bocchi pacem,: mentes hominum (ebrietas),: Agrippa discidio domum imminuerat,.—With acc. pers. only in Tac.: quamquam Augusta se violari et imminui quereretur,: perculso Seneca, promptum fuit Rufum Fenium imminuere,.—Hence, immĭnūtus, a, um, P. a., diminished, smaller, weak: mens,: modus intercalandi interdum cumulatior, interdum imminutior,

la:adj:immutatus.html:
immūtātus (inm-), a, um, adj.
2. in-mutatus
,
unchanged, unaltered (rare but class.): id mutavit, quia me immutatum videt,: veritas est, per quam immutata ea, quae sunt aut ante fuerunt aut futura sunt, dicuntur,.

la:verb:immuto.html:
immūto (inm-), āvi, ātum, 1 (archaic
inf. pres. pass. inmutarier, ; ; ), v. a.
in-muto
, to change, alter, transform.
In gen. (class.): ubi immutatus sum? ubi ego formam perdidi?: perscrutari ... nos nostri an alieni simus; ne clam quispiam nos imprudentis mmutaverit,: adeone homines inmutarier ex amore,: vultum earum,: imperio, potestate, prosperis rebus immutari,; cf.: me aliquando immutarunt tibi,: illi regi amabili Cyro subest ad immutandi animi licentiam crudelissimus ille Phalaris (v. ad), : ut ejus orbis (i. e. signiferi) unaquaeque pars alia alio modo moveat immutetque caelum,: concentus immutatus aut discrepans,: temeritas filii comprobavit; verborum ordinem immuta: fac sic: comprobavit filii temeritas, etc.,: nomen immuto,: cum successor aliquid immutat de institutis priorum,.—
In partic., in rhet.
To put, by metonymy, one word for another: immutata (verba), in quibus pro verbo proprio subicitur aliud, quod idem significet, sumptum ex re aliqua consequenti, etc. ... Ennius Horridam Africam terribili tremere tumultu cum dicit, pro Afris immutat Africam,; .—
E s p.: immutata oratio, allegory, = ἀλληγορία, .

la:verb:immutatus.html:
immūtātus (inm-), a, um, adj.
2. in-mutatus
,
unchanged, unaltered (rare but class.): id mutavit, quia me immutatum videt,: veritas est, per quam immutata ea, quae sunt aut ante fuerunt aut futura sunt, dicuntur,.

senses: monstrousness, enormity, fierceness, cruelty, barbarism, savageness, inhumanity, frightfulness
la:noun:immanitas.html:
immānĭtas, ātis, f.
immanis
.
Monstrous size, hugeness, vastness, excess (very rare, but class.): serpens inusitatae immanitatis,: vitiorum,: frigoris,.—
Monstrousness, enormity, heinousness, savageness, fierceness, cruelty, barbarism (so most freq.): ista in figura hominis feritas et immanitas beluae,: feritas quaedam atque agrestis immanitas,; cf.: multas esse gentes sic immanitate efferatas ut, etc.,: omni diritate atque immanitate taeterrimus,: inter feras satius est aetatem degere, quam in tanta immanitate versari,in such barbarism,: asperitas et immanitas naturae,: morum immanitate vastissimas vincit beluas,: in animo, stupor in corpore,; cf.: temperantiam immanitas in voluptatibus aspernandis imitatur,: M. Antonii tanta est non insolentia (nam id quidem vulgare vitium est), sed immanitas, non modo ut, etc.,: tanti facinoris immanitas,: parricidii,: priorum temporum,: ista verborum, (v. Madv. ad h. l.).

la:verb:immitto.gloss: to send, insert, introduce, into or against
senses: to send, insert, introduce, into or against
la:verb:immitto.html:
immitto (inm-), īsi, issum, 3 (
perf. sync. immisti, ), v. a.
in-mitto
, to send or let into a place, to introduce, admit, to send or despatch against, to let loose at, discharge at, to cast or throw into (freq. and class.; cf. intromitto, induco, introduco).
Lit.
In gen.: servos ad spoliandum fanum,; cf.: servi in tecta nostra cum facibus immissi,; : magna vis hominum simul immissa,: equitatu immisso (in agmen hostium),: armaturam levem in stationes,; : corpus in undas,: artificem mediis flammis,: completas naves taeda et pice in Pomponianam classem immisit,let loose,; so ib. § 5; cf.: navem in terram,: repente equum immisi ad eam legionem, urged, spurred, Galb. ap. : si effrenatos in eos equos immittitis,: pila in hostes,: tela,: telum ex manu,: canalibus aqua immissa,: aquam ex fullonicis in fundum vicini,: cloacam privatam in publicum,; and: puram aquam in alvum,: haec (tigna) cum machinationibus immissa in flumen defixerat,had driven into,: bipedales trabes, § 6: tigna (in parietem),; : coronam caelo,hurls it to the sky,: lentum filis immittitur aurum,is inserted, interwoven,: circa oneratas veste cervices laticlaviam immiserat mappam,put on, put around,: dexteraque immissis da mihi signa rotis,let loose, swiftly driven,; cf.: immissis pars caeca et concita frenis Arietat in portas,slackened,: habenas,; Ov. M. 1, 280; cf. rudentes,let go, let loose,: Codrus in medios se immisit hostes,threw himself,; : se in hostium manum multitudinemque,; cf.: immisit in armatas hostium copias,: offirmastin' occultare, quo te inmittas,whither you are going,. —
In partic.
To send against (secretly or hostilely), to set on, incite, instigate, suborn (mostly post-Aug.): alii Tarquinium a Cicerone immissum aiebant,: fratrem Tiberium inopinantem repente immisso tribuno militum interemit,; cf. : immissis qui monerent,: Suillium accusandis utrisque immittit,: ad cujus rei probationem immittet indices,: invidia et a dissimilibus delator inmissus,. —
To let grow unrestrained or wild: ea vitis immittitur ad uvas pariendas,: cupressus immittitur in perticas asseresve,: pro densitate arborum immissorumque aliorum in alios ramorum,grown together, interwoven,: penitus immissis radicibus niti, deeply planted or sunk, : barba immissa et intonso capillo, etc., overgrown, hanging down, Sisenn. ap. ; so, barba immissa,; ; : immissi capilli,; ; ; cf., in a Greek construction: Phleias immissus patrios de vertice crines,.—
To ingraft: trunci resecantur, et ... deinde feraces plantae immittuntur,.—
Aliquem in bona alicujus, to install, put in possession, .—
Trop.: aliquid in aures,to listen to,; but without in: ne tu quod istic fabuletur auris inmittas tuas,: verba suis immittere figuris, to accommodate its modes of thought to the words, : jactam et immissam a te nefariam in me injuriam semper duxi,: hic corrector in eo ipso loco, quo reprehendit, immittit imprudens ipse senarium,lets escape him,: si nihil extrinsecus accidit, quod corpus ejus in aliquam valetudinem immitteret,threw into some sickness,: immisitque fugam Teucris atrumque timorem,instilled, infused,: vires alicui,: amorem,.

la:adj:immanis.html:
immānis (inm-), e, adj.
i. e. in- and old Lat. mānus=bonus; kindr. with Sanscr. ma=metior, to measure; Lat. mānes, good spirits
,
monstrous in size, enormous, immense, huge, vast (class.).
Lit. (usually of inanim. and abstr. things): corporum magnitudo,; cf.: simulacra immani magnitudine,: immani corpore serpens,; : ingens immanisque praeda,: pecunia,: pocula,: immania ponti Aequora,: templa caeli,: antrum,; cf.: spelunca vasto hiatu,: barathrum,: tegumen leonis,: telum, al.: magna atque immanis,: cete,: numerus annorum,; cf.: exercitus,: frequentia amicorum,: geminos immani pondere caestus,: vox,: ambitus redit immanis: numquam fuit par,, b, 4: dissensio civitatis,: studium loquendi,: avaritia,: vitium,: soloecismus,: impulsae praeceps inmane ruinae,the vast crash,.—Neutr. absol.: Immane quantum animi exarsere, Fragm. ap. (2, 79 Dietsch); so, vino et lucernis Medus acinaces Immane quantum discrepat,how exceedingly, wonderfully,: civilis lapsu equi prostratus immane quantum suis pavoris et hostibus alacritatis indidit,: quod matrimonium Aemiliano huic immane quanto fuit, ; and in full: immane dictu est, quanti et quam multi ad Pompeium discesserint,.—
Trop., monstrous in character, frightful, inhuman, fierce, savage, wild (class.; syn.: ferus, immitis, barbarus, durus, saevus; opp. mansuetus, mitis): hostis in ceteris rebus nimis ferus et immanis,; cf.: nulla gens tam fera, nemo omnium tam immanis, cujus, etc.,: ex feris et immanibus mites reddidit et mansuetos,: ad humanitatem atque mansuetudinem revocavit animos hominum studiis bellandi jam immanes ac feros,: belua (with fera),; ; (with taetra),; cf.: immanis et vasta belua,: nihil ista immanius belua est,: janitor aulae, Cerberus,: ex hoc populo indomito, vel potius immani, etc.,: istius immanis atque importuna natura,: immanis, intolerandus, vesanus,: immanis ac barbara consuetudo hominum immolandorum,: tantum facinus, tam immane (patris occidendi),: coeptis effera Dido,: orae,: Raeti,: Agathyrsi,: Pyrrhus,.—Subst.: immānĭa, ium, n., frightful deeds or sayings: quamvis fabulosa et immania credebantur,stories however fabulous and frightful,: dira atque inmania pati,.—Comp.: scelere ante alios immanior omnes,.—Sup.: voluptatem immanissimus quisque acerrime sequitur,.—Hence, adv. in two forms, im-māne and immānĭter (not ante-Aug.).
(Acc. to I.) Monstrously, immoderately, excessively: immaniter clamare,.—More freq.,
(Acc. to II.) Frightfully, dreadfully, fiercely, savagely, wildly.
Form immane: leo hians immane,: sonat fluctus per saxa,; cf.: fremant torrentes,: spirans rapta securi,.—
Form immaniter: leones per ea loca saevientes immaniter, : perdite et immaniter vivere,.—
Comp.: immanius efferascunt,.

la:adj:immitis.html:
immītis (inm-), e, adj.
in-mitis
,
not soft or mellow, harsh, rough, sour (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic. or Cæs.).
Lit., of fruit: uva,: fructus (opp. dulcis),. —More freq.,
Transf., in gen., rough, rude, harsh, hard, severe, stern, fierce, savage, inexorable (syn.: barbarus, trux, torvus, immanis, ferox, crudelis, saevus): naturā et moribus immitis ferusque,; cf. asper et immitis,: arrogans, profusus, immitis,: tyrannus (i. e. Pluto),: Parcae,Glycera,: immitibus et desertis locis,: insulam Gyarum immitem et sine cultu hominum esse,: immite et turbidum caelum,: venti,: oculi,: nidi (i. e. hirundinum apibus infestarum),: ara (on which human beings are offered),: claustra,: vulnera,: fata,: mandata,: rescriptum,: mors,: caedes pariter fugientium ac resistentium,.—As subst.: immītĭa, ium, n., barbarous acts: ausae immitia nuptae (i. e. abortus),.—Comp.: vetus operis ac laboris, et eo immitior, quia toleraverat,; : calcato immitior hydro,.— Sup.: serpentes immitissimum animalium genus,.—Adv.: im-mīte, rudely, harshly: stridorque immite rudentum Sibilat,.

la:verb:immaneo.html:
immănĕo (inm-), ēre, v. n.
in-maneo
,
to remain in (late Lat.): cur non possit ... caelum levioribus immanere vaporibus? Aug. de Gen. ad lit. 2, 4 fin.

senses: unmoved, unshaken, undisturbed, immovable, firm, fixed, secure, steadfast
la:adj:immotus.html:
immōtus (inm-), a, um, adj.
in-motus
,
unmoved, immovable, motionless (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Lit.: (illa arbor) immota manet,: (Ceres) Sub Jove duravit multis immota diebus,: supercilia (opp. mobilia),: sceptrum,: aquae,i. e. frozen,: aër,: apum examina,: serenus et immotus dies,calm,; ; : terrarum pondus sedet immotum,: mare,: cervix,: legio,: vultus,. —
Trop., unmoved, unshaken, undisturbed, steadfast, firm: mens immota manet,: manent immota tuorum Fata tibi,; cf.: immota manet fatis Lavinia conjux,: immotas praebet mugitibus aures,unmoved,: nympha procis,: adversus turmas acies,; : immotus iis,: immota aut modice lacessita pax,: fides sociis,: felicis animi immota tranquillitas, Sen. de Ira, 2, 12, 6: constantia,: gaudium,: animus,.— In neutr.: si mihi non animo fixum immotumque sederet, Ne, etc.,immovable, unchangeable,; so with an object-clause: immotum adversus eos sermones fixumque Tiberio fuit non omittere caput rerum,.

la:adj:immensus.html:
immensus (inm-), a, um, adj.
inmensus
,
immeasurable, boundless, endless, vast, immense (freq. and class.; syn.: infinitus, ingens, interminatus).
Adj.
Lit.: si immensam et interminatam in omnes partes magnitudinem regionum videretis,: aëra deum statuit eumque gigni esseque immensum et infinitum,: ex ingenti quodam oratorem immensoque campo in exiguum sane gyrum compellitis,: in mari immenso vehi,: domus,: mons,: via,: fines ingenii,: series laborum,: jacuitque per antrum Immensus,; cf.: omnis eorum juventus infinita numero, immensa corporibus,: argenti pondus et auri,; : pretiis

emere, : observata sunt haec tempore immenso,: nox,.—

Trop., vast, measureless, boundless: morae,: fletus,: immensa vorago aut gurges vitiorum,: immensae, infinitae, immoderatae cupiditates,: sitis cruoris,: difficultas,: differentia,: fervet immensusque ruit profundo Pindarus ore, fathomless (the fig. being taken from a river), : immensum est, erratas dicere terras,there is no end of recounting,; cf.: quod persequi immensum est,.—Sup. (very rare): immensissimae voluptates,.—
Absol.
Subst.: immensum, i, n., a boundless extent, immense size, boundlessness, immensity (rare; not in Cic.): extra Processit longe flammantia moenia mundi, Atque omne immensum peragravit mente animoque,; cf. : loci,: per immensum ventis discordibus actus,: proruta per immensum aedificia,over a vast extent,: aliquid mercari immenso,at an enormous price,: mons saxeus in immensum editus,: ardet in immensum geminatis ignibus Aetne,: ad immensum aliquid augere,: aliquid immenso plus laudare,immoderately,. —
Adv.: immensum, without end, exceedingly, immensely (not freq. till after the Aug. per.): creverat immensum,: immensum attolli,: vigere,: luxus immensum proruperat,: immensum quantum hinc Oceano, illinc Hiberico mari conprimentibus,exceedingly,; .

la:adj:immeritus.html:
immĕrĭtus (inm-), a, um, adj.
inmeritus
,
undeserved (in the adj. mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Act., that has not deserved something, undeserving, guiltless, innocent: delicta majorum immeritus lues, Romane,; so of persons,; ; ; cf. gens,: urbes,: agni,: locus,: paries,: vestis,: arbor,ungues, (13).—With inf.: virtus recludens immeritis mori Caelum,.—Subst.: inmĕrĭ-tum, i, n., the absence of guilt or desert: cur tu, obsecro, immerito meo me morti dedere optas?for no fault of mine,; .—
Pass., that is not deserved, undeserved, unmerited (much less freq.): laudibus haud immeritis onerare aliquem,: credulus immerita Phasida juvit ope,: opes,: querelae,.—Hence, adv.: immĕrĭto (inm-), undeservedly, unjustly, without cause (esp. freq. with a negative): jam dudum te omnes nos accusare audio Immerito, et me omnium horunc immeritissimo,: si praeter opinionem, si immerito, si misera, si ingrata, etc., * : haud equidem immerito Cumanae carmine vatis Cautum,: ut eos non immerito probaverit sanctissimus censor,with perfect justice, justly,; so, non immerito,; ; ; 10, 1, 116; ; ; ; : neque immerito,; ; 7, 7, 1; 10, 1, 27; 11, 2, 1; 12, 10, 75: nec immerito,;

la:verb:immugio.html:
immūgio (inm-), īvi or ĭi, 4, v. n.
inmugio
,
to bellow, roar, or resound in or at (poet.): curvisque immugiit Aetna cavernis,: procella Antennae immugit,: maestoque immugit regia luctu,: judicaturo Domino lugubre mundus immugiet,.

la:adj:immemor.html:
immĕmor (inm-), ŏris (ante-class. in the
nom. sing. immemoris, Caecil. ap. Prisc. pp. 699 and 772 P.; Com. Fragm. v. 31 Rib.; abl. immemori, ; ; ; al. immemore,), adj.
in-memor
, unmindful, not thinking, forgetful, regardless, negligent of a thing.
Lit. (freq. and class.); constr. usually with gen.; less freq. absol. or with an inf.
With gen.: adeone immemor rerum a me gestarum esse videor?: hesternorum immemores, acta pueritiae recordari,: beneficii,: ne me immemorem mandati tui putares,: istius mandati tui,: hujus rei,: nec erat (L. Gellius) Romanarum rerum immemor,i. e. he was not ignorant of Roman history,: venator tenerae conjugis immemor,: immemor in testando nepotis,: omnium immemor difficultatum,: praedae,: sepulcri,: herbarum (juvenca),: graminis (cervus),; cf.: qua cibi qua quietis inmemor nox traducta est,: salutis immemores,.—
Absol.: magna haec immemoris ingenii signa,: immemori discedens pectore conjux,unfeeling,: mente,: possimne ingratus et immemor esse?; ; ; .—
With inf.: nihili est, suum Qui officium facere immemor est, nisi adeo monitus,; and with acc. and inf.: immemor, Chaeream Cassium nominari,never thinking, not considering,.—
Transf., that causes forgetfulness, a poet. epithet of Lethe, ; ; .

la:verb:immisceo.gloss: to mix in, blend, intermix, intermingle
senses: to mix in, blend, intermix, intermingle
to join, unite or associate with; mingle (amongst)
to take part in, interfere or meddle with
la:verb:immisceo.html:
immiscĕo (inm-), scŭi, xtum, or stum, 2 (archaic
inf. pres. pass. immiscerier, ) v. a.
in-misceo
, to mix in, intermix, intermingle, blend (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; not in Cic. or Cæs.).
Lit.: semina farinae,; ; sq.: vos meorum militum corpori immiscui,: elephanti per modica intervalla agmini immixti,: manus manibus,: summis ima,: sin maculae incipient rutilo immiscerier igni,: immixta corporibus semina,; cf. : immixtus castris hostium,: mediis se immiscuit armis,; cf.: feminas metus turbae virorum immiscuerat,: se nubi atrae,.—
Transf., to cling to: vestis immiscet cutem,.—
Esp.: se immiscere, or immisceri, to join, unite with any one, associate with: turbae servientium,: turbae sacricolarum,: manipulis,: cur immisceri sibi in cavea patres plebem nollent,: equites se peditibus,: ita se immiscuit mediis,: se hostibus,: veteribus militibus,; ; : vadimus immixti Danais,: se alienae familiae venali,; cf.: se pavonum gregi,.—
Trop.
In gen.: caelestibus immisceri,: si virtuti se voluptas immiscuisset,; : vera falsis,: sic enim vitia virtutibus inmixta sunt,: non fugienda petendis Immiscere,: quibus necessitudinibus immiscere te mihi parem,: immixtaque vota timori,: nec parvis periculis immixtus,.—
Esp.
To mingle, associate, connect one thing with another: sortem fortunae regnique sui cum rebus Romanis, (dub. Weissenb. ex conj. miscuisset).—
Se immiscere (immisceri) alicui rei, to take part in, concern one's self with, meddle with: fero et contionibus et comitiis se immiscere,; cf.: ne adfinitatibus, ne propinquitatibus immisceamur,: ne Philippus rebus Graeciae immisceretur,: cum se immiscuissent colloquiis montanorum,: Fidenati bello se jam ante immiscuerant,: se negotiis alienis,: se bonis hereditariis,.
la:verb:immisceo.inflection: scŭi, xtum, or stum, 2, v. a.

la:adj:immobilis.html:
immōbĭlis (inm-), e, adj.
in-mobilis
,
immovable.
Lit.
In gen. (class.): terra immobilis manens,: elephas tardum et paene immobile animal,: balaenae ad flexum,: rigor,: immobilior scopulis, .—
In partic.: res,immovable property, real estate,; ; opp. res mobiles,.—
Trop., immovable, unmoved, unalterable (mostly post-Aug.): ardet inexcita Ausonia atque immobilis ante,: donec princeps immobilem se precibus et invidiae juxta ostendit,: adversum plausum ac lasciviam insultantis vulgi immobiles,: isti apathiae sectatores, qui videri se esse tranquillos et intrepidos et immobiles volunt,: statua pro rostris cum hac inscriptione: PIETATIS IMMOBILIS ERGA PRINCIPEM,: omnia, quae mensurā continentur, certa et immobilia congruere sibi debent,.

la:verb:immolo.gloss: to sprinkle with the sacrificial meal (mola salsa)
senses: to sprinkle with the sacrificial meal (mola salsa)
to bring as a sacrificial offering
la:verb:immolo.html:
immŏlo (inm-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
inmola
.
Orig., to sprinkle a victim with sacrificial meal (mola salsa): olim hostiae immolatae dicebantur mola salsa tactae, cum vero ictae et aliquid ex illis in aram datum, mactatae dicebantur,.—So only in one other example in Cato: boves immolati, Cato ap. .—Far more freq. and class.,
Transf., to bring as an offering, to offer, sacrifice, immolate (cf. macto): ego hodie dis meis iratissumis sex agnos immolavi,: Musis bovem immolasse dicitur,: bovem Dianae,; cf.: Dianae vitulum,: hostias,: animalia capta,. 3: agnum,: aut pro victimis homines immolant aut se immolaturos vovent,: homines,; : filiam,: puerum,: qui hominem immolaverint, exve ejus sanguine litaverint, etc.,: porca, quae Cereri immolatur, Veran. ap. Paul. ex Müll.—Absol.: cum Sulla immolaret ante praetorium,: nemo nostrum est, quin, etiam cum de alia re immolaret, tamen, etc., Caecin. ap. : cum immolanti aufugisset hostia,; ; .—Pass. impers.:

cum pluribus dis immolatur, —With abl. of the offering: quibus hostiis immolandum cuique deo, cui majoribus, cui lactentibus, etc.,: itaque Jovi tauro, verre, ariete immolari non licet, Capit. ap. ; cf. ib. § 4.—

Poet., in a still more general sense, to sacrifice, slay: Pallas te hoc vulnere, Pallas Immolat,: inferias quos (juvenes) immolet umbris,; .—
(Eccl. Lat.) To present as an offering, render: humilitatem animae suae deo,: paenitentiam deo,: cui populus suffragiis immolat,does homage to,.

la:adj:immaturus.html:
immātūrus (inm-), a, um, adj.
inmaturus
,
untimely, before the season, unripe, immature (class.).
Lit., of plants and fruits: pira,: frons,: amomis,.—
Transf., of other things: vomica,: infans immaturus est editus,: puellae,i. e. not yet marriageable,: virgo,: sponsa,: mors,untimely, premature,; cf. ; ; : interitus C. Gracchi,: obitus,: iter mortis,: funus,; cf.: filius obiit,: puella,early dead,ossa,; : consilium,; : abi hinc cum inmaturo amore ad sponsum,unseasonable,.—Adv.: immātūrē, untimely, immaturely, ; ; fin.—Comp., .

la:verb:immulgeo.html:
immulgĕo (inm-), ēre, v. a.
in-mulgeo
,
to milk into: lacteam opem, Liv. And. ap. (Trag. Fragm. v. 38 Rib.): teneris immulgens ubera labris,: in dolore (oculi) et epiphoris si immulgeatur (lac), plurimum prodest,; .

la:adj:immunis.gloss: free or exempt from taxes, public service, or penalty (+ ablative)
senses: free or exempt from taxes, public service, or penalty (+ ablative)
la:adj:immunis.html:
immūnis (inm- and archaic in-moenis), e, adj.
in-munus
,
free or exempt from a public service, burāen, or charge (class.; cf.: expers, exsors).
Lit.: melius hi quam nos, qui piratas immunes, socios vectigales habemus,: quid immunes? hi certe nihil debent,: sine foedere immunes civitates ac liberae,, § 13; : immunis militiā,: Ilienses ab omni onere immunes praestitit,: qui agros immunes liberosque arant, i. e.,free from taxes, tax-free,; cf. : duo milia jugerum Sexto Clodio rhetori assignasti, et quidem immunia,.—
With gen.: immunes portoriorum,: ceterorum immunes nisi propulsandi hostis,.—
Transf., beyond the polit. and milit. sphere, free or exempt from, that contributes or gives nothing (mostly poet.): non cnim est inhumana virtus neque immunis neque superba,inactive,: quem scis inmunem Cinarae placuisse rapaci,who made no presents, without presents,; : Enipeus,: immunisque sedens aliena ad pabula fucus,doing nothing, idle,: ipsa quoque immunis rastroque intacta,without compulsion, free,.—In a play on the word: Ly. Civi inmuni scin quid cantari solet? ... Ph. Verum, gnate mi, is est inmunis, quoi nihil est qui munus fungatur suum, ; .—
With gen.: bos curvi immunis aratri,: immunes operum,.—
Trop., not sharing or partaking in, free from, devoid of, without any thing (poet. and in post-Aug. prose); constr. with gen., abl., with ab, or absol.
With gen.: aspicit urbem Immunem tanti belli,: tanti boni,: mali,: necis,exempt from,: caedis manus,free from, unstained with,: delictorum paternorum,: aequoris Arctos,not setting in, (an imitation of the Homeric ἄμμορος λοετρῶν Ὠκεανοῖο, Il. 18, 489); .—
With abl.: animum immunem esse tristitiā,: Cato omnibus humanis vitiis,: exercitum immunem tanta calamitate servavit,.—
With ab: immunis ab omnibus arbitris esse,: dentes a dolore,. —
Absol.: immunis aram si tetigit manus,stainless, pure,: amicum castigare ob meritam noxiam, Inmoenest facinus,a thankless office,; cf.: inmoene, improbum, culpandum, vel interdum munere liberatum, Gloss. Plac. p. 476.

immūtābĭlis (inm-), e, adj.

,
unchangeable, unalterable, immutable (rare but class.): esse causas immutabiles easque aeternas,; so, immutabilis et aeterna res,: nec magis immutabile ex vero in falsum,: res (with stabilis),: comprehensio (with stabilis),: spatia,: eadem ratio, quae fuit futuraque, donec res eaedem manebunt, inmutabilis est,: necessitas,: pondus verborum (with grave),.— Comp.: concordi populo nihil esse immutabilius, nihil firmius,.—Adv.: immūtābĭlĭter, unchangeably, ; App. de Mundo, p. 74.

la:verb:immoror.html:

Lit. (constr.: in aliqua re, alicul rei): ut saturae studiosius nidis immorentur,: puer meridiano inmorans,.—
Trop.: ne terrenis immorer,: honestis cogitationibus,: non exigo, ut immoriaris legationi, immorare, Auct. ap. : non arbitror mihi in hoc immorandum, quid sit, etc.,.

immergo (inm-), si, sum, 3 (
perf. sync. immersti, ; acc. to the second conj., inf. pres. pass. immergeri, ), v. a.
in-mergo
, to dip, plunge, sink, or stick into any thing, to immerse (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Lit.: manus in aquam ferventem,: immersus in flumen,: in aqua cui subinde (ferrum) candens immergitur,: nautas pelago,: partem arboris deflexam terrae,: aliquem spumosā undā,: immergi melle cotoneà,: manus,: se in aquam,: se alto (belua),.— Mid.: ubi Hister amnis inmergitur,i. e. pours itself into the sea,: at quidem tute errasti, quom parum inmersti ampliter (sc. manus),did not dip deep enough,.—
Transf., in gen.: se aliquo, to throw or plunge one's self into any thing, to betake one's self anywhere: immersit aliquo sese credo in ganeum,: se in contionem mediam,: inter mucrones se hostium immersit,.—
Trop.: se blanditiis et assentationibus in alicujus consuetudinem,: se studiis,: se penitus Pythagorae praeceptis,

,

Lit.: et in domum et in paternos hortos immigrabit,: in tam insolitum domicilium,: ubi illo (i. e. in aedes) immigrat,.—
Trop.: pleraque (verba) translata: sic tamen, ut ea non irruisse in alienum locum, sed immigrasse in suum diceres,: nulla res publica fuit, in quam tam serae avaritia luxuriaque immigraverint, Liv. prooem. § 11: posteaque immigravi in ingenium meum, i. e. gave myself up to it (the fig. being taken from a house; v. the passage in connection). .

la:noun:immunitas.gloss: freedom or exemption from taxes or public service
senses: freedom or exemption from taxes or public service
la:noun:immunitas.html:
immūnĭtas (inm-), ātis (
gen. plur. immunitatium, ), f.
immunis

Lit.: (Druides) militiae vacationem omniumque rerum habent immunitatem, * : immunitas et libertas provinciae,: immunitatem (a tributis) obtulit,; ; ; : personae quibus decimae immunitatem ipse (imperator) tribuit, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 16, 9, 3 et saep.—In plur., ,

1; ; ; ; .—

la:adj:immodestus.html:

inmodestus

unrestrained, excessive, extravagant, immoderate (rare but class.; syn. immoderatus): in vino. : mores,: largitione effundere,: fautores histrionum,: genus jocandi non profusum nec immodestum, * .—Advv.: immŏdestē.
